Executive Legislative Overview and Structural Architecture of the SR&ED Regime

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program constitutes the cornerstone of federal industrial and technological innovation policy in Canada, representing the single largest source of federal support for business-led research and development. Enacted within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR"), the program operates through a bifurcated fiscal delivery mechanism designed to subsidize both current operating outlays and capital investments dedicated to resolving scientific or technological uncertainties. First, section 37 of the ITA permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool and immediately deduct allowable SR&ED expenditures against income for tax purposes, or to carry unused expenditure pool balances forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in subsequent taxation years. Second, sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA generate Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) ranging from a baseline rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% of qualified SR&ED expenditures, which may be applied to reduce Part I federal tax otherwise payable, refunded directly in cash, carried back three taxation years, or carried forward up to twenty taxation years.

Governance of the federal SR&ED regime is divided between the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy and statutory amendments, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical and financial compliance through its specialized SR&ED Directorate. Because the incentive is delivered as an entitlement under the self-assessment income tax system rather than as a discretionary ministerial grant, any corporation, individual, trust, or partnership that satisfies the statutory criteria of subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 of the ITA within the prescribed statutory reporting deadline is legally entitled to the tax deduction and associated ITC.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential structural modernization since the 2012 federal budget reforms. Following two phases of national stakeholder consultations conducted by the Department of Finance between January 31, 2024, and May 27, 2024, the federal government unveiled sweeping legislative enhancements in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement, subsequently expanded through Budget 2025 and the August 2025 draft legislative proposals, enacted by the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, assented to March 26, 2026), and reflected in the CRA's updated Investment Tax Credit Policy in October 2026. These reforms fundamentally altered four structural pillars of the federal regime for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). First, the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC rate was doubled from $3 million to $6 million. Second, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds governing the reduction of the expenditure limit for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) were expanded from the historic $10 million–$50 million corridor to a substantially wider $15 million–$75 million corridor, accompanied by a new statutory election permitting CCPCs to calculate their expenditure limit phase-out using a three-year average gross revenue test instead of taxable capital. Third, access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC rate up to the $6 million expenditure limit was extended for the first time to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), subject to a mandatory phase-out between $15 million and $75 million of three-year average annual gross revenue calculated on a consolidated group basis. Fourth, the eligibility of capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (and lease costs first becoming payable on or after that date)—which had been repealed since January 1, 2014—was restored for both the section 37 income deduction pool and the section 127 ITC, carrying a 40% refundability rate on the resulting capital ITCs for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs.

Simultaneously, the federal government redirected its intellectual property (IP) commercialization tax policy away from an income-based "Patent Box" regime. Although the Department of Finance conducted formal consultations on a Patent Box from January 31, 2024, to April 15, 2024, and the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement signalled an intent to introduce such a measure, both Budget 2025 (tabled November 2025) and Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) omitted a Patent Box regime entirely. Budget 2026 instead proposes, for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, to extend SR&ED eligibility to tests, technological validations and studies needed to obtain the initial regulatory approval or certification required to commercialize a product or process (where directly related to an eligible SR&ED project), and to the costs of registering and maintaining intellectual property protection, such as patents, for intellectual property developed in an eligible SR&ED project. In its place, federal tax policy pivoted toward upfront capital recovery through the Productivity Super-Deduction introduced in Budget 2025 and the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction (announced on September 15, 2026, and released as draft legislation on October 1, 2026), which would establish immediate 100% capital cost allowance (CCA) expensing across more than 65% of business capital assets, encompassing patents, software, cloud computing infrastructure, data network equipment, and qualifying manufacturing facilities, alongside $2.4 billion in sovereign artificial intelligence (AI) compute and adoption funding.

body.text: Statutory Framework Under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations
The Subsection 248(1) Definition of Scientific Research and Experimental Development

The legal threshold governing entry into the Canadian R&D tax system is codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statute stratifies qualifying investigations into three mutually reinforcing functional categories, while explicitly enumerating qualifying support work and excluded commercial or routine activities. Under paragraphs (a) through (c) of the definition in subsection 248(1), the core investigative work must consist of basic research, defined in paragraph (a) as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research, defined in paragraph (b) as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; or experimental development, defined in paragraph (c) as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In corporate practice, more than 90% of Canadian industrial claims fall within paragraph (c) (experimental development), where the statutory inclusion of "incremental improvements" ensures that evolutionary technological progress—rather than solely disruptive or paradigm-shifting invention—qualifies for relief, provided the work seeks an advancement in the underlying technology rather than merely applying existing engineering knowledge.

Once a core basic research, applied research, or experimental development project is established, paragraph (d) of the definition in subsection 248(1) extends eligibility to work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. This statutory linkage is critical: computer programming, CAD modelling, or physical testing conducted in isolation does not constitute SR&ED; however, when executed directly in support of resolving a technological uncertainty within an eligible experimental development project, and scaled strictly to the requirements of that investigation ("commensurate with the needs"), the entire supporting effort is absorbed into the statutory perimeter of the SR&ED project.

Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition in subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude specific commercial, routine, and non-scientific activities from qualifying as SR&ED. Specifically, the statute bars claims for work with respect to market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; or routine data collection.
The Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool and Loss Restriction Mechanics

Section 37 of the ITA establishes the mechanics for deducting allowable SR&ED expenditures in computing a taxpayer's income from a business for a taxation year. Rather than requiring R&D expenses to be capitalized and amortized over the useful life of resulting intangible assets, or forcing current deductions that might expire as non-capital losses after twenty years, subsection 37(1) aggregates a taxpayer's domestic SR&ED expenditures into a dedicated, cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.

Under paragraph 37(1)(a), the pool includes all expenditures of a current nature made by the taxpayer in the taxation year (or a preceding taxation year ending after 1973) on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer. Following the amendments proposed in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and enacted by S.C. 2026, c. 3, paragraph 37(1)(b) was amended to restore the inclusion of capital expenditures made by the taxpayer for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, that is intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more of its operating time) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or whose value is all or substantially all consumed in that prosecution.

The subsection 37(1) expenditure pool operates as a running balance computed at the close of each taxation year on Part 3 of Form T661. Additions to the pool comprise current-year allowable current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a), current-year allowable capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024, under paragraph 37(1)(b), repayments in the year of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and Form T661 Schedule B, and prior-year unclaimed pool balances brought forward. Reductions to the pool encompass government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received in respect of SR&ED at the filing due date under paragraph 37(1)(d), plus the amount of federal SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded in the immediately preceding taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e).

A critical timing asymmetry is governed by paragraph 37(1)(e): whereas provincial R&D tax credits and direct grants (such as NRC IRAP) constitute government assistance that reduces the section 37 expenditure pool and the qualified expenditure base in the current taxation year (the year in which the underlying expenditure is incurred), the federal SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded in Year 1 reduces the section 37 deductible expenditure pool in Year 2. If the Year 1 federal ITC reduction causes the subsection 37(1) pool balance in Year 2 to become negative, the negative balance is reduced to zero on Form T661 and the absolute value of the negative amount must be included in the taxpayer's business income in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA.

Furthermore, while an unused subsection 37(1) expenditure pool balance can otherwise be carried forward indefinitely, subsection 37(6.1), operating in conjunction with paragraph 37(1)(h), imposes a strict "loss restriction event" (acquisition of control) limitation. When control of a corporation is acquired by a person or group of persons, the corporation's unused subsection 37(1) SR&ED deduction pool from pre-acquisition taxation years is streaming-restricted: it can only be deducted in post-acquisition taxation years if the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit throughout the post-acquisition year, and only up to the amount of the corporation's income for that year from that same business (or a similar business where substantially all of the income is derived from the sale, leasing, rental, or development of similar properties or the rendering of similar services).

With respect to cross-border R&D, section 37(2) permits a current income deduction for expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada (which are excluded from the subsection 37(1) pool and generally ineligible for ITCs), while subsection 37(1.4) provides a narrow exception allowing salaries or wages of Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED outside Canada to be included in the domestic subsection 37(1) pool and to earn ITCs, up to a maximum cap of 10% of the total salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year, provided the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer, is integral to a domestic SR&ED project, and is not subject to foreign income or profits tax.
The Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit and Refundability Framework

Once a taxpayer's allowable SR&ED expenditures are established under section 37, section 127 of the ITA governs the conversion of those expenditures (plus the Prescribed Proxy Amount, if elected) into "qualified expenditures" eligible to earn Investment Tax Credits. Under subsection 127(5), a taxpayer may deduct from Part I tax otherwise payable for a taxation year an amount not exceeding the taxpayer's "investment tax credit" at the end of the year. Subsection 127(9) defines the "investment tax credit" pool as encompassing 15% of the taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year, plus unused ITCs carried forward from the preceding 20 taxation years or carried back from the subsequent 3 taxation years.

For eligible domestic corporations, subsection 127(10.1) provides an addition to the investment tax credit equal to 20% of the lesser of the corporation's qualified SR&ED expenditures for the year and its annual "expenditure limit" for the year. Combining the 15% basic ITC under subsection 127(9) with the 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1) yields the 35% enhanced ITC rate. Prior to the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, subsection 127(10.1) applied exclusively to corporations that were Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) throughout the taxation year. Pursuant to S.C. 2026, c. 3, subsection 127(10.1) was amended to apply equally to a corporation that is an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) throughout a taxation year beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

To prevent abuse of the ITC regime through artificial intra-group asset churn or premature commercialization of subsidized capital assets, subsections 127(27) through 127(35) enforce SR&ED ITC recapture rules. If a taxpayer acquires a property for which an SR&ED ITC was claimed (or transfers qualified expenditures under a non-arm's length contract) and, within 20 taxation years (10 years under certain provincial equivalents such as British Columbia), converts the property to commercial use or disposes of it without the property having been previously converted to commercial use, a percentage of the original cost or proceeds of disposition is recaptured and added directly to the taxpayer's Part I federal tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion. Subsections 127(33) to 127(35) provide a deferral relief mechanism where a non-arm's length transfer of SR&ED property to another taxpayer would otherwise trigger immediate recapture: subsection 127(33) disapplies subsections 127(27) to 127(29) to the transferor, and subsections 127(34) and 127(35) instead apply recapture to the purchaser (or purchasing partnership) when it later converts the property to commercial use or disposes of it.

Finally, section 127.1 of the ITA transforms unused SR&ED ITCs from non-refundable tax offsets into direct cash refunds ("refundable investment tax credit"). Under subsection 127.1(1), a taxpayer's refundable ITC for a taxation year is deemed under paragraph 152(1)(b) to be a payment on account of Part I tax payable, generating a cash refund to the extent it exceeds the taxpayer's actual tax liabilities. Pursuant to subsection 127(5), any SR&ED ITC refunded in the taxation year is deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable, thereby extinguishing that portion of the ITC pool and preventing double utilization via carryforward or carryback.
Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, and the 2024–2026 Reforms
Expansion to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations and the $6 Million Expenditure Limit

For decades, a major structural criticism of Canada's innovation tax architecture was the harsh fiscal cliff faced by high-growth Canadian technology and life sciences companies upon executing an initial public offering (IPO). The moment a CCPC listed its shares on a designated stock exchange (such as the Toronto Stock Exchange or TSX Venture Exchange), it ceased to be a CCPC under subsection 125(7) of the ITA, causing its SR&ED ITC rate to plummet from 35% (100% refundable) to 15% (0% refundable). Consequently, many pre-revenue or R&D-intensive Canadian firms delayed public listings or became acquisition targets for foreign multinationals, prompting the Department of Finance to centre its 2024 SR&ED consultations on retaining domestic intellectual property and supporting scaling Canadian public companies.

The resulting reforms, effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), introduced the statutory category of the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) in subsection 127(9) and new subsection 127(10.6) of the ITA. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy four cumulative conditions: first, it must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year; second, it must be a public corporation (having a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada, or having elected or been designated as a public corporation under subsection 89(1) of the ITA) throughout the taxation year, or a corporation that would be a public corporation if its shares listed on a designated stock exchange outside Canada were taken into account; third, it must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (de jure or de facto control under subsection 256(5.1)), by one or more non-resident persons throughout the taxation year; and fourth, it must not be a corporation that would be controlled by a particular person if each share owned by a non-resident person were owned by that particular person. The definition also extends to an eligible subsidiary, being a corporation resident in Canada at least 90% of whose shares are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more eligible Canadian public corporations.

Concurrently, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the 35% enhanced ITC rate was increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for both CCPCs (under amended subsection 127(10.2)) and ECPCs (under new subsection 127(10.6)). While the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed an intermediate expenditure limit of $4.5 million, Budget 2025 and the subsequent legislative enactments elevated the final statutory cap to $6 million retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. At the 35% rate, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC with $6 million in current SR&ED expenditures can now generate up to $2,100,000 in fully refundable federal cash tax credits annually, double the previous maximum of $1,050,000.

Where a CCPC or ECPC has a short taxation year (shorter than 51 weeks), the $6 million expenditure limit (or $3 million for pre-December 16, 2024 years) is prorated strictly by the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365:
Prorated Expenditure Limit = Expenditure Limit × (Number of Days in Taxation Year ÷ 365)

Furthermore, the $6 million expenditure limit cannot be multiplied across related entities. For CCPCs, the expenditure limit must be shared and allocated among all CCPCs in an "associated group" (as determined under section 256 of the ITA) using Schedule T2SCH49. For ECPCs, the expenditure limit must be shared among all members of a consolidated group that prepare "consolidated financial statements" as defined in subsection 127(9)—meaning financial statements in which the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the members of the group are presented as those of a single economic entity. Special anti-avoidance rules apply where an ECPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is a member of a consolidated group in two or more of those taxation years.
Phase-Out Mechanics: Taxable Capital vs. Elective Three-Year Average Gross Revenue

Historically, a CCPC's expenditure limit was subject to a dual phase-out based on both prior-year taxable income and prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. For taxation years ending after March 19, 2019, the federal government repealed the taxable income phase-out, leaving prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (between $10 million and $50 million) as the sole reduction mechanism for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the phase-out architecture was overhauled to expand the phase-out corridor from $10M–$50M to $15 million–$75 million and to introduce a gross revenue phase-out metric alongside taxable capital across three distinct statutory pathways.

Under the CCPC Default Method (Taxable Capital Employed in Canada under subsection 127(10.2)), unless a CCPC elects otherwise, its $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when its taxable capital employed in Canada (calculated under Part I.3 principles, sections 181.2 to 181.4 of the ITA, aggregated across all associated CCPCs) for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated (reduced to nil) once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. Expressed mathematically, for a full 365-day taxation year beginning on or after December 16, 2024:
Expenditure Limit<sub>CCPC (Capital)</sub> = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − max(0, TC<sub>prior</sub> − $15,000,000)) ÷ $60,000,000]

where TC<sub>prior</sub> is the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the preceding taxation year (capped at $75,000,000, at which point the limit equals $0). For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula used a base limit of $3,000,000 and phased out over the $40,000,000 span between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital.

Under the ECPC Mandatory Method (Three-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue under subsection 127(10.6)), a revenue-based test replaces the capital test. Because public corporations frequently raise substantial equity capital on public markets to fund multi-year clinical trials, deep-tech hardware development, or AI infrastructure—which immediately inflates share capital and retained earnings (the core components of taxable capital under Part I.3) long before the company generates commercial revenue—applying a taxable capital test to public corporations would disqualify virtually all mid-cap biotech and technology issuers. Consequently, subsection 127(10.6) mandates that an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out based on its average annual gross revenue over the preceding three fiscal years, as reflected in its financial statements (or the consolidated financial statements of its consolidated group if the ECPC is a member of a consolidated group). The straight-line reduction begins when the three-year average annual gross revenue exceeds $15,000,000 and reaches zero at $75,000,000:
Expenditure Limit<sub>ECPC (Revenue)</sub> = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − max(0, Rev<sub>3-yr avg</sub> − $15,000,000)) ÷ $60,000,000]

If an entity leaves or joins a consolidated group during the year, the average annual revenue used is that of the consolidated group as reflected in the consolidated financial statements for the year in question.

Under the CCPC Elective Method (Three-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue Election under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32)), private corporations are granted access to the same revenue metric. Venture-backed private corporations (CCPCs) that have raised large Series B, C, or D preferred equity rounds or convertible debt often exceed $15 million or even $75 million in taxable capital employed in Canada while remaining pre-revenue or early-revenue. To prevent private venture-backed CCPCs from being disadvantaged relative to ECPCs, the post-December 15, 2024 rules permit a CCPC to elect (on the prescribed form) to compute its expenditure limit phase-out using the ECPC three-year average annual revenue method rather than the taxable capital method. Where a CCPC is associated with one or more other CCPCs, all members of the associated group must jointly elect to use the revenue method, and the calculation aggregates the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of each corporation that is a member of the associated group for the taxation year in question over the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout the entirety of that three-year period.
Comprehensive Refundability Matrix Across Corporate Classifications

Under section 127.1 of the ITA, the rate at which an earned SR&ED ITC is refunded in cash depends on three intersecting variables: the legal classification of the claimant corporation (Qualifying Corporation, Excluded Corporation, Subsection 127.1(2.01) CCPC, ECPC, or general corporation), whether the underlying expenditure falls within or exceeds the corporation's annual expenditure limit, and whether the expenditure is of a current nature or a capital nature (for property acquired after December 15, 2024).

In subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA, a Qualifying Corporation is defined as a CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (together with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their taxation years ending in the same calendar year) does not exceed the corporation's qualifying income limit, which phases out based on prior-year taxable capital. Conversely, an Excluded Corporation is defined as a corporation that is, at any time in the year, controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more persons exempt from Part I tax under section 149, by His Majesty in right of a province, a Canadian municipality or any other public authority, or by any combination of such persons, or that is related to any such person. Finally, a Subsection 127.1(2.01) CCPC is a CCPC that is neither a Qualifying Corporation nor an Excluded Corporation—typically a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeded the qualifying income limit due to a profitable year or capital gain, but whose taxable capital remains below the $75 million phase-out ceiling, allowing it to retain an expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2). Prior to the repeal of the taxable income phase-out in 2019, this distinction was narrower; today, subsection 127.1(2.01) ensures that a high-income CCPC still receives a 100% refund of its 35% ITC on current expenditures up to its expenditure limit, and a 40% refund of its 35% ITC on capital expenditures up to its expenditure limit, although it receives 0% refundability on the 15% ITC earned on expenditures exceeding its expenditure limit.

Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Calculation Methodologies, and Statutory Restrictions
Salaries and Wages, Specified Employee Caps, and Unpaid Remuneration Rules

In Canadian SR&ED claims, salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada typically represent 70% to 85% of total qualified expenditures. Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) or (B) of the ITA, eligible remuneration includes gross salaries, wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, and the employer's share of statutory payroll remittances (Canada Pension Plan [CPP], Québec Pension Plan [QPP], Employment Insurance [EI], provincial employer health taxes, and Workers' Compensation Board [WCB/WSIB] assessments) to the extent they relate to time spent directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED.

However, the ITA and ITR impose stringent restrictions on specified employees and unpaid remuneration. A "specified employee" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as an employee of a person who is a specified shareholder of the person—meaning a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, not less than 10% of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any other corporation that is related to the corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer, such as a spouse, child, sibling, or parent of a controlling shareholder. Under the direct SR&ED salary cap in subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, bonuses and remuneration based on profits for a specified employee are completely disallowed as SR&ED expenditures. Furthermore, the maximum amount of a specified employee's salary or wages that may be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure in a taxation year is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is employed by the taxpayer. Any excess is deemed under subsection 37(9.1) not to be an expenditure on SR&ED.

When computing the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the proxy method, an even stricter cap applies to specified employees under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9) of the ITR. Specifically, subsection 2900(7) of the ITR restricts the maximum amount included in the PPA salary base for a specified employee to the lesser of two thresholds: first, 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (comprising both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 of the ITA, and prior year's unpaid salary paid in the current year under subsection 78(4)); or second, 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days of employment in the year, determined by the statutory formula:
PPA Specified Employee Cap = 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365)

where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual, with no proration for any portion of the year during which the employee was not a specified employee. If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in the same year, the cap must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).

In addition to specified employee restrictions, accrued and unpaid remuneration is strictly policed under subsection 78(4) of the ITA. Where an amount in respect of salary, wages, or other remuneration is accrued and unpaid at the end of a taxation year, it is only deductible in that taxation year if it is actually paid before the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year. If an accrued SR&ED salary remains unpaid on the 180th day following fiscal year-end, it is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year; instead, it is deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid, reported on Line 315 as an exclusion in Year 1 and claimed on Line 310 of Form T661 in the year of payment. Critically, under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, prior-year unpaid salaries that are paid and claimed in a subsequent year on Line 310 are permanently excluded from the PPA salary base, meaning the claimant forfeits the 55% proxy overhead uplift on any SR&ED salary that misses the 180-day payment window.
Overhead Cost Recovery: The Prescribed Proxy Amount vs. The Traditional Method

A defining feature of the Canadian SR&ED regime is the statutory election provided under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) (the Traditional Method) and clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) (the Proxy Method) of the ITA for capturing overhead and indirect supporting expenditures. The claimant must select one method for the entire taxation year in Part 1 of Form T661 (Field 160 for Proxy or Field 162 for Traditional), and this election is irrevocable once the Form T661 for the year has been filed.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not itemize or track actual SR&ED overhead expenses. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional overhead figure—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661. Pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the ITR, since January 1, 2014 (following step-down reductions from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013), the PPA equals 55% of the eligible salary base. The salary base consists solely of the portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and subsection 78(4) late-paid salaries, and subject to the subsection 2900(7) specified employee caps. Two structural rules govern the PPA. First, the PPA is not added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; the actual overhead expenses that the PPA represents (such as office rent, utilities, human resources, clerical support, and indirect supervisory time) are deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA, while the notional 55% PPA is added exclusively to "qualified SR&ED expenditures" in Part 4 of Form T661 to generate federal and applicable provincial ITCs. Second, the PPA is subject to an Overall Cap calculated as A − B − C under subsection 2900(6) of the ITR, where A is the total amount deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold), and B and C represent specific statutory deductions (such as direct SR&ED expenditures, CCA, building rent, and interest) that cannot constitute SR&ED overhead. This prevents a pre-operational startup with minimal actual overhead deductions from claiming a notional PPA that exceeds its total non-SR&ED business expenses.

Under the Traditional Method, governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR (read in conjunction with the prescribed exclusions in section 2902 of the ITR), the claimant foregoes the 55% PPA and instead identifies, proves, and claims actual overhead and other expenditures that meet one of two statutory tests. The expenditures must be either directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (including other expenditures under paragraph 2900(2)(c) that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED—meaning the expense would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not occurred), or directly attributable (and directly related and incremental under paragraph 2900(3)(b)) to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

body.text: Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, Non-Arm's Length Transfers, and Materials

Beyond internal payroll and overhead, the SR&ED framework regulates three external expenditure categories: contract SR&ED (subcontractors), third-party payments, and physical materials consumed or transformed. Where a claimant engages an arm's length Canadian contractor to perform SR&ED work directly on the claimant's behalf in Canada (including both core subsection 248(1)(a)–(c) investigations and subsection 248(1)(d) directly supporting work), 100% of the contract expenditure is deductible in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool. However, since January 1, 2013 (pursuant to Budget 2012 amendments to subsection 127(9)), only 80% of an arm's length contract expenditure is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures for calculating the ITC. This 20% haircut removes the subcontractor's presumed profit margin from the federal tax credit base. Claimants must itemize all arm's length (Line 340) and non-arm's length (Line 345) contracts exceeding $30,000 on Form T661. Conversely, payments to non-resident subcontractors performing R&D outside Canada are completely ineligible for both the subsection 37(1) domestic pool and the SR&ED ITC, though they remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 37(2) or section 9.

Where a claimant pays a non-arm's length party (such as a parent, subsidiary, or sister corporation) to perform SR&ED, the payment does not automatically qualify for an ITC in the hands of the payer. Instead, under subsection 127(13) of the ITA, the non-arm's length performer incurs the qualified expenditures and may transfer all or part of those qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the payer by jointly executing and filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) with their respective Form T661 filings. If the non-arm's length contractor simply supplies general services that do not in themselves constitute SR&ED (such as renting crane time or routine machining), the cost is evaluated under subsection 127(11.6) at the non-arm's length provider's actual cost without markup.

Payments made by a corporation to an approved association, an approved university, college, research institute, or other similar approved organization, or to a non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada, to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the taxpayer (and where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results of that SR&ED) qualify as third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii). Unlike contract SR&ED, where the contractor performs work on behalf of and under the direction of the claimant, third-party payments fund autonomous research by an approved entity or consortium. Each third-party payment must be reported on Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED, formerly Schedule A to Form T661), and like arm's length subcontracts, 80% of the payment qualifies for the SR&ED ITC.

Expenditures for physical materials under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR qualify for 100% inclusion in both the section 37 pool and the ITC calculation if the materials are either consumed or transformed. Materials consumed are those destroyed, rendered virtually valueless, or exhausted during the prosecution of SR&ED, such as chemical reagents, biological media, or destructive test specimens. Materials transformed are those integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig constructed during SR&ED, even if that prototype or product may eventually possess some residual value. However, if a prototype or transformed material is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED ITC recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(30) apply to claw back the ITC on the lesser of the fair market value or proceeds of disposition of the transformed materials and the original material cost claimed. Utilities, cloud computing subscriptions, and software-as-a-service (SaaS) licences do not constitute physical "materials consumed or transformed"; under current CRA policy, cloud computing costs incurred to train AI models or run simulations are ineligible under the Proxy Method (as they are considered overhead or equipment lease equivalents covered by the PPA) and may only be claimed under the Traditional Method if they satisfy the strict "directly related and incremental" test under paragraph 2900(2)(c) or 2900(3)(b) of the ITR.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Integration With the Productivity Mega Deduction

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (depreciable property) and equipment lease costs were wholly excluded from the SR&ED regime. For property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, the amendments to paragraph 37(1)(b), subsection 127(9), and section 127.1 enacted by S.C. 2026, c. 3 (alongside the repeal of paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1)) fully restore the pre-2014 capital expenditure rules. Under the All or Substantially All (ASA) capital property rule, depreciable property (other than a building or leasehold interest in a building) acquired on or after December 16, 2024, that is intended to be used during all or substantially all (≥ 90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualifies for a 100% immediate deduction under paragraph 37(1)(b) and earns the 35% enhanced ITC (up to the $6M expenditure limit for CCPCs and ECPCs), refundable at 40%. Lease costs of equipment first payable on or after December 16, 2024, qualify where the equipment is used all or substantially all (≥ 90%) for SR&ED under either the Proxy or Traditional method; if the leased equipment is used primarily (> 50% but < 90%) for SR&ED, 50% of the lease cost qualifies if the taxpayer elects the Proxy Method, whereas 0% qualifies if the taxpayer uses the Traditional Method.

Alongside the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures, Canadian taxpayers benefit from two major Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) immediate expensing regimes introduced in 2024–2026 for innovation and productivity assets that do not meet the 90% SR&ED use threshold, or that include buildings and intangible IP. First, the Budget 2024 Immediate Expensing for Productivity-Enhancing Assets provides a 100% first-year CCA deduction for property in Class 44 (patents or a right to use patented information for a limited or unlimited period), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software, such as laptops, servers, and GPU clusters) acquired after April 15, 2024, and that becomes available for use before January 1, 2027. Second, the Productivity Mega Deduction—which expands the Productivity Super-Deduction introduced in Budget 2025 and was unveiled on September 15, 2026, released as formal draft legislation on October 1, 2026, and featured as a flagship measure of Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) in response to the United States' One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)—would expand 100% immediate CCA expensing across more than 65% of business capital assets. This encompasses manufacturing or processing buildings located in Canada acquired on or after November 4, 2025, and used before 2030 where at least 90% of the floor space is used for manufacturing or processing, as well as patents, software, cloud computing infrastructure, laboratory equipment, and testing or validation equipment, while providing a 50% enhanced first-year Accelerated Investment Incentive write-off for general commercial assets.
Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Grant Stacking Mechanics

To prevent taxpayers from recovering more than 100% of an R&D expenditure through overlapping government programs, paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(11.5) of the ITA enforce mandatory reductions for "government assistance" and "non-government assistance" (as defined in subsection 127(9)) as well as "contract payments". Any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, investment allowance, or provincial R&D tax credit that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the time of filing in respect of SR&ED must be subtracted from both the section 37 expenditure pool and the qualified SR&ED expenditure base before calculating the federal ITC.

When "stacking" non-dilutive direct grants—most notably the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—with SR&ED tax credits, a precise mathematical interaction occurs under the Proxy Method. While the NRC IRAP grant directly reduces the qualified SR&ED expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661, the PPA in Part 5 of Form T661 is calculated on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base prior to deducting government assistance in Part 4; consequently, an NRC IRAP wage reimbursement does not reduce the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount.

This interaction is demonstrated by examining a Canadian SaaS startup employing 10 developers with $800,000 in eligible direct SR&ED salaries, electing the 55% Proxy Method, and receiving an NRC IRAP contribution covering 80% of $400,000 of those salaries ($320,000 grant). Under a simplified direct-offset view (excluding proxy overhead), the $320,000 IRAP grant reduces the $800,000 R&D spend to $480,000 (or, if evaluating a $400,000 unfunded tranche separately, a 35% SR&ED ITC on $400,000 yields $140,000, which combined with $320,000 IRAP and a $20,000 training grant recovers $480,000, or 60% of the $800,000 spend). When incorporating the statutory 55% PPA on the full $800,000 direct salary base ($800,000 × 55% = $440,000 PPA), total gross expenditures plus PPA equal $1,240,000. Subtracting the $320,000 IRAP assistance leaves $920,000 in net qualified SR&ED expenditures (prior to provincial tax credit assistance), generating $322,000 in federal SR&ED ITC at 35%, which combined with the $320,000 IRAP grant yields $642,000 in combined federal recovery, representing 80.25% of the $800,000 cash payroll outlay.
Judicial Precedents, Technical Eligibility Criteria, and Administrative Audit Governance
The Northwest Hydraulic Five-Question Jurisprudence and the CRA Two-Requirement Framework

While subsection 248(1) of the ITA provides the statutory text for SR&ED, Canadian courts have forged the operational doctrine used to distinguish eligible experimental development from routine engineering or standard software development. The foundational judicial authority in Canada is the decision of Justice Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (T.C.C.).

In Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman articulated five cumulative criteria (historically referred to across CRA administrative literature as the "Five Questions") that a taxpayer must satisfy on a balance of probabilities to establish that claimed activities constitute SR&ED under subsection 248(1). The first criterion asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; Justice Bowman emphasized that the term "routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, meaning that if the problem can be resolved by applying established engineering principles or standard debugging, no technological uncertainty exists. The second criterion asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, which requires a five-stage cognitive and operational progression: the observation of the subject matter, the identification of a technological problem, the formulation of a verifiable hypothesis, the testing of that hypothesis by experiment or analysis, and the logical formulation of conclusions. The third criterion asks whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses, such that trial-and-error tinkering without systematic analytical rigour fails the test. The fourth criterion asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; crucially, Justice Bowman established that a technological advancement does not require commercial success or even a working prototype, as the conclusive rejection of a reasonable hypothesis—proving scientifically why a particular technological pathway fails under specific constraints—advances the baseline of technological knowledge and satisfies the statutory requirement. Finally, the fifth criterion asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed; while the ITA does not prescribe a specific template for technical records, Justice Bowman noted that it is virtually impossible to prove a systematic scientific investigation in the absence of contemporaneous experimental logs, test results, code commits, design iterations, or engineering notebooks generated as the work progressed.

In August 2021 (and reaffirmed through August 2025 updates), the CRA published its consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, which reorganized the Northwest Hydraulic five questions into Two Overarching Requirements—the "Why" and the "How". As the CRA explicitly states in its policy history, both the two requirements and the five questions are derived directly from the unchanged statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and provide a common language for claimants and CRA officials.

body.text: Dual-Track CRA Audit Architecture: Research and Technology Advisors and Financial Reviewers

The Canada Revenue Agency administers the SR&ED program through a specialized, dual-track review architecture housed within its SR&ED Directorate across regional Tax Services Offices, pairing technical specialists with financial auditors. On the technical track, Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) are CRA officers holding university degrees and industry experience in engineering, computer science, biotechnology, physics, chemistry, or manufacturing. Operating under the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors and Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants, the RTA's mandate is to evaluate Part 2 of Form T661, conduct on-site or virtual technical interviews with the claimant's lead engineers or scientists, inspect contemporaneous evidence, and issue a Technical Review Report determining whether each claimed project satisfies the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED, as well as whether claimed support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) is commensurate with the needs of the eligible core work.

On the financial track, Financial Reviewers (FRs) are CRA tax auditors who operate under the SR&ED Program Financial Claim Review Manual – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers. Working in concert with the RTA, the FR verifies that all claimed expenditures on Part 3, Part 4, Part 5, and Part 6 of Form T661 are substantiated by books and records (general ledgers, T4 slips, payroll registers, time-tracking sheets, subcontractor invoices, cancelled cheques, and Form T1145, T1146 or T1174 agreements), applies the specified employee caps and subsection 78(4) unpaid wage rules, verifies government assistance deductions, and prepares a signed Financial Review Report (or Short Financial Review Report) with a complete Table of Contents and working paper file.
Audit Selection, Mandatory Review Thresholds, Proposal Letters, and Appellate Remedies

Historically and currently, approximately 60% to 70% of SR&ED claims are accepted as filed following initial automated risk-scoring and desktop screening at the CRA Tax Centre, while approximately 20% to 30% of claims are referred to a local Tax Services Office for a coordinated technical and/or financial audit. Under the CRA's SR&ED Program Financial Claim Review Manual, specific mandatory oversight and quality-control thresholds govern the audit file. Enhanced senior review and mandatory reporting protocols apply to any SR&ED audit file where the permanent income change exceeds ±$2,000,000, where the permanent tax change exceeds ±$400,000, where the net present value of the Tax Earned By Audit (TEBA-NPV) exceeds ±$400,000, or where the net present value of the Tax Protected Changes (TPRO-NPV) exceeds ±$1,000,000. Where a claimant's documentation is deficient, the CRA Assistant Director (AD) is empowered under Chapter 5.12.7 of the Manual (and subsection 230(3) of the ITA) to issue a formal legal requirement to maintain better books and records, placing the taxpayer on formal notice for subsequent taxation years.

If the RTA or FR proposes adjustments (denying projects in whole or in part, or reducing allowable expenditures and ITCs), the CRA issues a formal Proposal Letter accompanied by a Summary of Adjustments. The claimant is afforded 30 days to submit written technical or financial representations, or to sign and return the Summary of Adjustments indicating concurrence. In the working paper file, the FR must explicitly document one of four outcomes: that the claimant agrees with the proposed adjustments (via a signed Summary of Adjustments or confirmation letter); that the claimant does not agree with some or all of the proposed adjustments; that the claimant has made representations, but it is not clear whether there is concurrence; or that the claimant has not responded orally or in writing.

Once the CRA finalizes its review and issues a Notice of Reassessment (or, where a claimant requested a refundable ITC by filing an amended return or Tax Preparatory Request [TPR] with no SR&ED claim in the original T2 return and the ITC is denied in full, a Notice of Determination of the deemed payment on account of tax payable under paragraph 152(1)(b) of the ITA), the claimant has a strict statutory deadline of 90 days from the date of the Notice to file a formal Notice of Objection (Form T400A) addressed to the Chief of Appeals at their Tax Services Office. If the CRA Appeals Division confirms the reassessment or fails to vacate or vary it within 90 days, the taxpayer may appeal directly to the Tax Court of Canada. Furthermore, under the Taxpayer Relief (Fairness) provisions, the Minister may grant relief from penalties or arrears interest where extraordinary circumstances (flood, fire, serious illness), undue delays by the CRA in completing a review, or documented financial hardship exist.
Statutory Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, Deadlines, and Preparer Penalties
The Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline and Prescribed Form Architecture

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m) of the ITA, a taxpayer's SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. For corporations, because a T2 income tax return filing due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after the end of its taxation year (even though any balance of corporate tax owing is due 2 months after year-end, or 3 months after year-end for an eligible CCPC claiming the small business deduction under paragraph 157(1)(b)), adding the 12-month SR&ED reporting window yields an absolute deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For an individual carrying on an unincorporated business (whose T1 return is due June 15 of the following calendar year), the SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the December 31 taxation year-end (June 15 of the second following year), whereas for trusts (whose T3 return is due 90 days after the trust's year-end), the SR&ED deadline is 15 months after year-end. Where SR&ED is undertaken by or on behalf of a partnership, Form T661 must be filed on behalf of the partnership no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing due dates for the return of income of the members for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ended, and corporate partners claim their proportionate share of the ITC; partnerships themselves cannot earn the 35% enhanced CCPC or ECPC rate, and must deduct the SR&ED expenditures at the partnership level before allocating net partnership income or loss to partners.

The 18-month corporate reporting deadline is statutory and absolute. If a claimant fails to file Form T661 and the applicable ITC schedule (Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals and trusts) containing the prescribed information for an expenditure by the 18-month deadline, that expenditure is permanently barred from inclusion in the subsection 37(1) pool and permanently disqualified from earning an ITC under section 127. Neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada possesses discretionary authority under the fairness provisions of subsection 220(3.1) to waive or extend the 18-month filing deadline. However, the subsequent deduction of an amount from an already-established subsection 37(1) expenditure pool is not subject to the 18-month deadline, provided the underlying expenditures were timely reported on Form T661 in the year incurred.

body.text: Technical Narrative Requirements on Form T661 Part 2 and the 20-Project Filing Election

Form T661 is structured into ten distinct parts (Part 1 through Part 10). Part 2 (Project Information: Sections A to C) captures the scientific and technological narrative for each claimed project. Section B of Part 2 enforces strict electronic word limits designed to compel concise, technically rigorous descriptions written in the language of the qualified personnel who performed the work. Specifically, Line 242 asks what scientific or technological uncertainties the claimant attempted to overcome, subject to a maximum of 350 words, and must define the capability gap or system-level constraint in the underlying science or technology that could not be resolved through standard practice or publicly available knowledge. Line 244 asks what work was performed in the tax year to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties described in Line 242, subject to a maximum of 700 words, and must detail the systematic investigation chronologically—the hypotheses formulated, experimental configurations or analytical models built, parameters tested, test results observed, and iterative modifications executed during the specific fiscal year. Line 246 asks what scientific or technological advancements were achieved or attempted as a result of the work described in Line 244, subject to a maximum of 350 words, and must articulate the new scientific or technological knowledge generated through the investigation, including knowledge gained from failed experiments.

Under Section 4.1 of the CRA's Filing Requirements Policy, a claimant with more than 20 SR&ED projects in a single taxation year may elect to submit Part 2 project descriptions with their tax return for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value. However, three strict conditions apply to this administrative relief: first, the cost of every project claimed (not merely the top 20) must be itemized and reported in Part 6 (Project Costs) of Form T661 by the 18-month reporting deadline; second, the claimant must complete and maintain at their place of business a full Part 2 of Form T661 for all projects claimed; and third, upon CRA request during a review, the claimant must immediately submit the completed Part 2 for any or all of the remaining projects, failing which the expenditures for those projects will be summarily disallowed.

Furthermore, if a federal agency has designated any of a claimant's SR&ED projects as "classified information" for national security reasons, the claimant must complete all parts of Form T661 (completing Section B of Part 2 on a separate sheet kept on file rather than transmitting it with the return) and send a formal notification letter to the Technical Guidance Division of the SR&ED Directorate in Ottawa, including a copy of that letter with the tax return. Because commercial corporate tax software transmits all prescribed Form T661 fields electronically, electronic filers must not submit duplicate paper copies of Form T661.
Claim Preparer Disclosure Mandates and Joint and Several Penalty Liability

Introduced in Budget 2013 and codified in subsections 162(5.1) to (5.3) of the ITA, Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) of Form T661 mandates comprehensive transparency regarding third-party SR&ED consultants and tax advisors. Every claim preparer who has accepted (or agreed to accept) consideration to prepare or assist in the preparation of the SR&ED claim must be identified in Part 9, along with their CRA Business Number, billing arrangement code (such as contingency fee, flat fee, or hourly rate), the exact contingency percentage or fee rate (contingency fees in the Canadian market commonly range from 15% to 25% of the claim value), and the total fee paid or payable.

If any prescribed information in Part 9 regarding the claim preparer(s) or billing arrangement(s) is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, subsection 162(5.1) imposes a statutory $1,000 penalty. Crucially, where a claim preparer has prepared or assisted in preparing the form, the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable for the $1,000 penalty. However, unlike Parts 2, 3, 4, and 6, Part 9 is not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline, and an omission or error in Part 9 will not invalidate or disallow the underlying SR&ED claim.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes Across Canada

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, almost all Canadian provinces and the Yukon Territory offer supplementary R&D tax incentives. Except for Québec and Alberta (which administer their own corporate tax systems through Revenu Québec and Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, respectively), provincial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA under federal-provincial Tax Collection Agreements and piggyback on the federal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) and federal Form T661 filings. Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, any provincial R&D credit earned in the taxation year reduces the federal qualified expenditure base, unless the taxpayer formally renounces the provincial credit by the filing deadline.

body.text: Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario's R&D tax architecture comprises three distinct, stackable credits governed by the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, claimed on Schedule 566) provides an 8% refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to a $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit, generating up to $240,000 in cash refunds. The $3 million Ontario expenditure limit phases out when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000, or when its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lies between $25 million and $50 million. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC, claimed on Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations (both CCPCs and non-CCPCs) with a permanent establishment in Ontario on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures. Because the OITC is deducted from the eligible expenditure base prior to calculating the ORDTC, a qualifying CCPC claims the 8% OITC first and then claims the 3.5% ORDTC on the remaining 92% of its Ontario expenditures (an effective additional 3.22% non-refundable credit), with unused ORDTC balances eligible for a 20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback, or formal waiver/renunciation to avoid reducing the federal 35% refundable ITC base when the corporation is in a loss position. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC, claimed on Schedule 568) provides a 20% refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs on up to $20 million of qualified expenditures incurred under eligible research contracts with approved Ontario post-secondary institutions, hospital research institutes, or non-profit research centres, yielding up to $4 million in cash refunds.
Québec: Revenu Québec Administration and Transition From RD-1029.7 to the Unified CRIC Regime

Québec operates the most autonomous R&D tax system in Canada, administered directly by Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec) via the CO-17 corporate tax return and Form RD-222 (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures). Unlike the federal Proxy Method, Québec does not use a 55% notional overhead proxy; instead, Québec historically focused its primary tax credit directly on R&D salaries, wages, and 50% of subcontractor payments.

For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Québec's regime centred on Form RD-1029.7 (Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D)), supplemented by specialized credits for university or public research centre contracts (Form RD-1029.8.6), research consortium fees (Form RD-1029.8.9.03), and private partnership pre-competitive research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1). Under Form RD-1029.7, Canadian-controlled corporations with total assets under $50 million earned a 30% refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of eligible Québec R&D wages, phasing down linearly to 14% for assets between $50 million and $75 million, and fixed at 14% for large or foreign-controlled corporations. However, eligible expenditures were reduced by an asset-based exclusion threshold ranging from a base of $50,000 (for corporations with assets ≤ $1M) up to $225,000 (for assets ≥ $14M), with a $12,500 threshold rule applicable in specific partnership contexts.

In the Québec 2025–2026 Budget, the Québec Ministry of Finance enacted a sweeping consolidation of its innovation incentives effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing the legacy RD-1029.7 and specialized R&D credits with the unified CRIC (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation / Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization), claimed on Form RD-222 and Form RD-1029.8.CR. The CRIC introduces a unified rate structure across all corporate sizes, abolishing the distinction between CCPCs and large, public, or foreign-controlled corporations. Every corporation carrying on R&D in Québec receives a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures (in excess of the exclusion threshold), and a 20% fully refundable tax credit (up from 14%) on all eligible expenditures exceeding $1,000,000. In addition to R&D salaries and subcontractor outlays, the CRIC expands the eligible expenditure base to include pre-commercialization expenditures (such as regulatory homologation, certification testing, industrial design, and late-stage commercialization prototyping that fall outside federal subsection 248(1) boundaries) as well as capital expenditures for property used in R&D and pre-commercialization in Québec. Finally, the CRIC replaces the legacy $50,000–$225,000 asset-scaled exclusion threshold (and the former $83,333 university salary cap) with a hybrid exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or an employee-based threshold calculated using the Québec basic personal income tax amount multiplied by the proportion of time each employee devotes to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.
British Columbia: Harmonized 10% SR&ED Tax Credit Under Bill 2

Governed by Part 6 (section 97) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act and recently amended by Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) enacted pursuant to the 2026 B.C. Budget, the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit provides a 10% tax credit on B.C. qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a corporation with a permanent establishment in British Columbia; individuals are ineligible, though qualifying corporations that are active members of a partnership may claim their proportionate share of the non-refundable credit.

Through Bill 2 (updated April 2026), British Columbia fully harmonized its provincial SR&ED credit with the 2024–2025 federal SR&ED reforms for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) may now claim a 10% refundable tax credit on the lesser of their B.C. qualified SR&ED expenditures and their federal expenditure limit, which increased from $3 million to $6,000,000, yielding up to $600,000 in refundable B.C. credits. Concurrently, B.C. increased the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor for CCPCs to $15 million–$75 million (and adopted the federal ECPC expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.6)) and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures as B.C. qualified expenditures. Expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit (and claims by other corporations or partnership members) earn a 10% non-refundable credit that can be carried back 3 years or forward 10 years, or formally renounced. B.C. imposes a 10-year recapture rule if SR&ED property is disposed of or converted to commercial use. The credit is claimed on Form T666 (reported on Schedule 5 lines 659 and 674) and must be filed with the CRA no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant Incremental Base-Spending Model

Effective January 1, 2021, Alberta replaced its previous provincial SR&ED tax credit with the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), delivered directly through the Alberta corporate income tax system via AT1 Schedule 29 under the policy leadership of the Ministry of Technology and Innovation and Alberta Treasury Board and Finance. Operating alongside Alberta's 8% general corporate income tax rate (the lowest in Canada) and 2% small business rate, the IEG utilizes a two-tier incremental structure on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D expenditures that match federal SR&ED eligibility criteria. Under the first tier, corporations receive an 8% refundable grant payment on eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's "base level of spending," defined as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years. Under the second tier, corporations receive an enhanced 20% refundable grant payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds their two-year average base spending level, up to the $4 million total expenditure cap. Thus, a newly formed Alberta startup with $0 in R&D spending in its prior two years, or an expanding firm rapidly scaling its R&D team, earns the full 20% refundable rate on its incremental Alberta R&D expenditures. The $4 million maximum expenditure limit under the Alberta IEG phases out incrementally for corporations with taxable capital between $10 million and $50 million, and corporations with $50 million or more in taxable capital are completely ineligible.
Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Canada, and Yukon R&D Tax Incentives

Across the Prairie provinces, Atlantic Canada, and the North, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits provide substantial refundable liquidity that integrates directly with the federal SR&ED calculation. Saskatchewan provides a 10% refundable R&D tax credit (Schedule 403) for CCPCs on the first $1 million of qualifying Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures, and a 10% non-refundable credit for non-CCPCs and CCPC expenditures above $1 million, subject to a combined $10 million annual expenditure cap. Governed by section 7.3 of the Manitoba Income Tax Act (Schedule 380), Manitoba provides a 15% Research and Development Tax Credit (reduced from 20% for expenditures incurred after April 11, 2017) with no expenditure cap. For in-house R&D carried out in Manitoba, half of the credit (7.5%) is refundable and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable (eligible for a 20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback); where the R&D is performed under contract with an eligible Manitoba post-secondary educational institution or research institute, the entire 15% credit is fully refundable. Finally, Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301), and the Yukon Territory (Schedule 442) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to all corporations regardless of size, ownership, or taxable capital, with no annual expenditure cap, while Yukon provides an additional 5% bonus credit, totalling 20%, on R&D payments made to Yukon University.
Strategic Synthesis, Policy Trajectory, and Compliance Risk Management

The post-December 2024 statutory evolution of the Canadian R&D tax regime—highlighted by the doubling of the 35% enhanced expenditure limit to $6 million, the widening of the phase-out corridor to $15 million–$75 million, the inclusion of Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), the introduction of the elective three-year average gross revenue test for CCPCs, the restoration of capital expenditure eligibility, and the enactment of the 2025 Québec CRIC and the proposed 2026 federal Productivity Mega Deduction—creates three interconnected strategic imperatives for corporate tax executives and R&D auditors.

First, corporate tax planners must perform an annual optimization of the CCPC phase-out election between taxable capital and three-year average gross revenue. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, capital-intensive or venture-financed CCPCs whose balance-sheet equity and debt push their prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15 million (and up to or beyond $75 million) must model the new subsection 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) elections to use the three-year average annual gross revenue method. For a pre-revenue or early-revenue biotechnology, clean-technology, or deep-tech CCPC with $80 million in venture equity on its balance sheet, filing the prescribed joint election across its associated group restores its expenditure limit from $0 to the full $6,000,000, unlocking up to $2.1 million in refundable federal cash credits, plus up to $600,000 in harmonized British Columbia refundable credits.

Second, financial controllers must execute a synchronized capital expenditure allocation between the restored SR&ED capital regime and the Productivity Mega Deduction. With paragraph 37(1)(b) SR&ED capital expenditure eligibility (for equipment used ≥ 90% in SR&ED acquired on or after December 16, 2024) now enacted and the October 2026 Productivity Mega Deduction (100% immediate CCA expensing across > 65% of business assets, including patents, software, cloud infrastructure, and 90%+ manufacturing buildings acquired on or after November 4, 2025) proposed, tax planners must rigorously segregate capital assets at acquisition. Equipment meeting the 90% SR&ED use test should be routed into Form T661 to capture both the 100% section 37 deduction and the 35% or 15% SR&ED ITC (with 40% cash refundability for CCPCs and ECPCs), whereas shared-use R&D hardware (< 90% SR&ED use), commercial cloud and data network infrastructure, patent acquisition costs, and manufacturing facilities should be routed into the Productivity Mega Deduction and Budget 2024 immediate expensing CCA classes (Classes 44, 46, 50, and 53) to achieve 100% first-year tax depreciation without triggering SR&ED recapture risks upon subsequent commercial deployment.

Third, claimants must institutionalize contemporaneous audit defence and statutory deadline discipline. As maximum refundable claim sizes double from $1.05 million to $2.1 million (at the federal level), a significantly higher proportion of mid-market claims will cross the CRA Financial Claim Review Manual’s key review thresholds (e.g., ±$400,000 permanent tax change or TEBA-NPV, or ±$2,000,000 permanent income change). Sustaining eligibility under combined RTA and FR scrutiny requires integrating the Northwest Hydraulic and CRA "Why and How" documentation framework directly into engineering workflows—tracking hypothesis-driven commits, test logs, and project-level time allocation contemporaneously—while paying all accrued R&D salaries strictly within the 180-day subsection 78(4) window, executing non-arm's length Form T1146 and T1174 agreements on time, and enforcing internal compliance calendars well ahead of the absolute 18-month statutory filing deadline.
